 Minimum-Wage Employment Costs to Rise by Over £4,000 Within Three Years
 Minimum Wage UK minimum-wage employment costs to rise by over £4,000 Annual cost for a 21-year-old climbs £4,462 Youth rate rises slower, ending a Labour pledge Loading Stock video by Kiwi and Camera via Pexels 
 Nov 4, 2026 
 Minimum-Wage Employment Costs to Rise by Over £4,000 Within Three Years
 The yearly expense of employing a minimum-wage worker is set to rise by more than £4,000 within three years, according to analysis reported by Yahoo Finance . Research by the Centre for Policy Studies indicates that from April 2027, companies will pay an additional £4,462 annually to hire a 21-year-old on the minimum wage compared with 2024. 
 The analysis found that the cost of employing a worker on the National Living Wage for 35 hours a week will reach £26,898 a year, up from £22,438 two years earlier. At the recent Budget, John Healey confirmed that the National Living Wage, which sets the minimum for those aged 21 and over, would increase from £12.71 to £13.21 per hour.
 Healey also announced that the rise in the youth rate of the minimum wage would be smaller than in previous years, setting aside a 2024 Labour manifesto commitment. Labour had pledged to eliminate what it described as discriminatory youth rates by raising them faster than the adult rate.
 Employers have cautioned that increases in minimum wage rates for under-21s and under-18s since Labour took office have made hiring younger workers less attractive. Office for National Statistics figures showed the unemployment rate for 16 to 24-year-olds at 15.6pc in the three months to August 2026, compared with 13.8pc in the same period of 2024.
 Unemployment rate, aged 16 and over (seasonally adjusted, three-month average), United Kingdom 4.70% · Jul 2026 · ▼ 0.2 pp 3% 4% 5% 6% 2022 2023 2024 2025 2026 Source: Office for National Statistics (UK) 1Y 3Y All Download Share Open on IndexBox 
 Daniel Herring, head of fiscal and economic policy at the Centre for Policy Studies, credited Healey for slowing the rise in the youth minimum wage but said the government had continued to increase pressure on businesses during a difficult period. Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, raised the minimum wage for 18 to 20-year-olds by 8.5pc to £10.85 per hour in April this year, more than double the increase for those aged 21.
 The youth rate increase means the cost of employing an 18-year-old has risen by £4,859 a year between 2024 and April 2027. Healey's Budget measure will lift the youth rate to £11.27, a 3.9pc rise matching the pace for those aged 21 and older. Herring added that the increase in the National Living Wage follows a decade of above-inflation rises in the cost of employing someone on the minimum wage.
